patches.old: The behavior cannot be classified as a disorder solely because it is absent from the DSM-5
patches.new: No specific DSM-5 diagnosis applies, because the manual's recognised categories rather than the 4D framework determine formal diagnosis

patches.old: The DSM-5 serves as the official diagnostic manual, and a behavior not listed in it cannot receive an official diagnosis regardless of how many criteria for abnormality it appears to meet.
patches.new: The DSM-5 is the manual that defines formal diagnoses, so a presentation matching none of its categories does not receive a specific diagnosis no matter how many abnormality criteria it appears to meet. In practice the DSM-5 anticipates exactly this situation: it provides **other specified** and **unspecified** categories within each chapter so that a clinically significant presentation which does not fit a listed disorder can still be recorded and treated.

visual.title: How a diagnosis is built, and what it costs
visual.alt: Four cards setting out the components of a DSM entry — symptom counts, duration, impairment and exclusions — with the note that they exist to make clinicians agree; a comparison of reliability, which the criteria bought, against validity, which remains unsettled given comorbidity and the absence of confirmatory tests; a list of the four Ds with the caveat attached to each; and a panel on labelling covering the Rosenhan study and the three levels of stigma alongside the benefits a diagnosis brings.
visual.caption: The criteria were written to make two clinicians agree. Agreement is reliability; whether the category is real is a separate question, and still open.
